chief_complaint: progressive cape-like pain and temperature loss in arms years after spinal cord injury
hpi_details: 47M with history of thoracic paraplegia from MVC 10 years ago presenting with new ascending numbness and hand weakness due to expanding central spinal cord syrinx.
ideas: He thinks he has developed pinched nerves in his neck or severe carpal tunnel from a decade of pushing his wheelchair.
concerns: He is worried he is losing the strength in his arms and hands, which would take away the last bit of independence he has left.
expectations: He hopes to get an MRI of his neck and a referral for physical therapy or hand splints to keep his hands functioning.
pmh: Thoracic spinal cord injury with paraplegia after MVC 10 years ago; hypertension and mild dyslipidemia

teaching.one_liner: Years after a spinal cord injury, a fluid-filled cyst can slowly expand within the cord above the original injury level, causing new ascending numbness and hand weakness—a delayed complication that needs new imaging, not dismissal as 'just the old injury'.
differentials: Progression of original spinal cord injury (less likely to be new)
red_flags: New symptoms above the level of the original injury—a syrinx-specific warning sign

must_ask.say: Is this numbness and weakness new, different from your usual symptoms since the injury?
Where exactly do you feel the numbness? Does it feel like a cape over your shoulders?
Have you noticed new weakness in your hands?
When and how did your original spinal cord injury happen?
How has this been changing over recent weeks or months?

history.answer: My arms have been getting numb and I've been losing strength in both of my hands over the last few months.
It feels like a combination of both—a dull numbness over my shoulders and arms, plus noticeable weakness when I try to grip things with my hands.
It covers both of my shoulders, goes down both arms into my hands, and spreads across the upper part of my chest like a shawl or cape.
I noticed I cannot tell hot water from cold water on my arms, and I accidentally burned my forearm on a coffee pot without feeling the heat, though I can still feel someone touching me.
It began very gradually about five or six months ago, not suddenly.
It has been slowly creeping upward and getting worse over time, affecting my hands more and more.
Ten years ago, I was in a car crash that injured my mid-back and paralyzed both of my legs, but until recently, my arms and hands were completely normal.
Yes, that's what terrifies me—my baseline injury was down in my mid-back around my chest, so having new symptoms up in my neck, shoulders, and arms is completely new.
I have been dropping drinking glasses and struggling to button my shirts or fasten zippers because my fingers feel clumsy and weak.
Coughing, sneezing, or bearing down hard while transferring to my wheelchair seems to give me a weird fullness or ache in my neck and arms, but it doesn't change with the time of day.
I have a dull ache across the back of my neck and upper back, but no sharp shooting shocks down the arms.
No, my speech is totally clear, my face does not droop, I have no vision problems, and I have not had any dizziness.
No, I have no trouble swallowing, no chewing fatigue, no eyelid drooping, and my breathing feels completely fine.
I have used intermittent catheterization and a bowel routine since my spinal injury ten years ago, and there has been no change in that baseline.
I have not noticed muscle twitching, but the fleshy parts between the bones on the back of my hands look a little thinner than they used to.
No, I haven't had any stomach bug, diarrhea, fever, or cold symptoms recently.
I push my manual wheelchair every day, but I haven't changed my routine, and I don't rest on my elbows or bend my wrists awkwardly.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, but I don't have diabetes, heart rhythm problems, or any heart disease.
No, I eat a regular balanced diet with meat, I've never had stomach surgery, and I don't drink alcohol heavily.
I only take Lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure; I don't take water pills, steroids, or chemotherapy drugs.
I thought I just pinched a nerve in my neck or got carpal tunnel from wheeling myself around for ten years.
I'm terrified of losing my hands, because if my arms stop working, I won't even be able to feed myself or transfer out of bed.
I'm hoping for a neck scan and a referral for physical therapy or braces so I can keep using my hands.
Aside from my thoracic spinal cord injury with paraplegia from the car crash ten years ago, I just have high blood pressure and mild dyslipidemia.
I had spinal stabilization surgery and extensive rehabilitation ten years ago after the car accident, but no other surgeries since.
I have no known drug allergies.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco.
I might have a single glass of wine on special occasions, but essentially I don't drink.
I work remotely as an accountant, live in an accessible home, and am completely independent with my wheelchair.
My father had high blood pressure, but there are no nerve disorders or spinal diseases in my family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 °C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and capillary blood glucose 102 mg/dL.
Alert, comfortable male seated in a manual wheelchair, in no acute distress, with normal speech and facial symmetry.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact, with symmetric facial movements, no ptosis, intact extraocular motility, normal visual fields, and symmetric palate elevation.

Mild intrinsic hand muscle wasting and bilateral hand grip/finger abduction weakness (grade 4/5) with normal shoulder and elbow strength (5/5), alongside baseline flaccid paraplegia (0/5) in both legs.
Suspended cape-like loss of pinprick and temperature sensation across the shoulders, arms, and upper chest, with preserved light touch and proprioception, and complete baseline sensory loss below T6.
Biceps and brachioradialis reflexes diminished (1+) bilaterally, triceps reflexes 1+ bilaterally, and hyperactive patellar/Achilles reflexes (3+) with bilateral positive Babinski signs.
Well-healed surgical scar along the mid-thoracic spine, no cervical spine tenderness, negative Spurling test bilaterally, and negative seated straight-leg raise.
